# dsh-split-workspaces

A local DSH plugin bundle: it tiles several workspaces **side by side and stacked** in the
main pane

l of the Harness Web UI, one workspace conversation per pane. Splitters can be
dragged to resize, ti

tle bars can be dragged to swap two panes' positions, and the pane
that currently holds focus is mar
ked by a brand-coloured title bar.
## What it adds

- One row of icons in the sidebar (two tiled squares, right next to the Plugins icon);
clicking it s

witches the main area to the **multi-workspace tiled** panel.
- The panel itself: at the top are the

title and `Add workspace`, below is the
board — every pane has its own title bar (workspace name an

d path, the `Open directory`
icon, the `Replace workspace` icon, the `Split` icon, mode selector, se

ssion selector,
close), and inside the pane it
reuses the shared `conversation.content` Factory (the

`embedded` variant), mounted under an
explicit `SessionProvider` binding, so each pane is a complet

e conversation (transcript,
input box, streaming output).
- **The `Open directory` icon** (the folde

r to the right of the workspace name): clicking it
hands **that pane's** workspace directory to the

system file manager (Linux `xdg-open`,
macOS Finder, Windows Explorer). It does not implement this m

achinery itself; instead it
reuses the two methods of the already-installed Session remote namespace

(`@deepseek-ai/dsh-api-session-controller`): `canOpenWorkspacePath()` first answers
"can this deplo

yment hand a path to the desktop" (a Linux container with no graphical
environment answers false, wh

ich is exactly what "there is no file manager in front of
you" means), and then `openWorkspacePath({

path })` **validates** in the composite
filesystem that this path really is a directory the Host ca

n open, and opens it according
to the operating system's association — a directory's association is

the file manager.
So "which command to use to open it" has only one implementation and one set of
va

lidations, and this plugin does not have to add a row on the Host or make users restart.
Availabilit

y is a deployment-level fact and is asked only once; a directory that is not in
the Host mapping, a

file manager that will not start, a deployment with no session
service, or no graphical environment

at all are each spelled out in the pane's own error
line (the localised reason first, the Host's ori

ginal text appended as detail).

## Design mode: draw the delegation tree as arrows

The panel has two modes: **tile** (the default, everything described above) and **design**.
Design m

ode draws every **session** as a card and connects them with arrows into a directed
tree — the arrow

direction *is* the delegation direction, and deleting an arrow revokes the
authorization. There is
no second configuration: the graph is the permission.

- **Draw one**: drag from the dot on a card's right edge onto another card.
- **Delete one**: click

the small cross at the arrow's midpoint.
- **Sessions, not panes**: the same session opened in two p

anes still has one card, and
closing a pane never deletes an arrow. Only deleting the session drops

has one card, and
closing a pane never deletes an arrow. Only deleting the session drops its edges.

Two invariants keep it a tree: no cycles, and at most one parent per session. Both are
enforced by a
pure function (`validateEdge`) before the edge is added.
### The `dispatch_task` tool

A session with outgoing arrows gets an **agent-scoped** copy of `dispatch_task` (it shadows
the glob
al one) whose description lists the available targets.
| Parameter | Meaning |
| `task` | Task body. The target cannot see A's history, so background **and verifiable acceptance c
riteria** belong here. Omit it when waiting for a previous dispatch. When the target is already runn

ing, a `task` means a **correction** (queued to its next round, no new goal) |
| `targets` | Array o
f targets. Each item may be an index, full title, title fragment, or session id. Required when more
than one target is available; omitted with no `task`, it means "keep waiting on everything still run

ning" |
| `wait` | `all` (default) / `any` (return on the first deliverable) / `none` (do not wait)

ing" |
| `wait` | `all` (default) / `any` (return on the first deliverable) / `none` (do not wait) |

The call returns a batch: `{ status, results, stillRunning, note }`, where `results` holds one
`{ ta

rget, status, deliverable, reply, progress, interruptedBy, note }` per target in request
order. **On

ly a `deliverable: true` reply is a conclusion.** Text from `running` / `blocked` /
`paused` / `inte

rrupted` goes into `progress`, explicitly marked as a draft that later rounds may
overturn; `interru
ptedBy: "user"` means the user stopped the target.

What happens: split new dispatches, continuations and corrections → **preflight every new
target's i

dleness (one busy target rejects the whole new batch)** → create a **goal** on the
target session vi

a `goals.create` (so it keeps working across rounds instead of replying once) →
wait according to `w

ait` → shape the results. A call waits at most 5 minutes at a time and
returns `running` with `progr

ess` (`deliverable: false`); the model calls again with no arguments
to keep waiting. A call that se
nds `task` to a running target returns `redirected` instead.

`wait: 'none'` returns immediately with `dispatched` (or `redirected` for a correction) and keeps
a

background watcher that records the conclusion. Because a dispatch must not be forgotten, the
owner

is nudged once per turn at `agent/turn-stopping` — injected into the next step, so the same

### Boundaries worth knowing

- **Multiple targets run in parallel**, each with its own waiter; results come back in request
order

. The tool never guesses "probably all of them" — name them when there is more than one.
- **One tas

k per target at a time.** A `task` sent to a running target is a **correction**, not a
second task:

it is queued via `sessions.prompt(mode: 'queue')`, creates no new goal, and returns
`redirected`. Do

not mix corrections and new dispatches in one call.
- **A user stop is reported as `interrupted`.**

A `turn/end` with `aborted.user` closes the
dispatch immediately (`interruptedBy: "user"`, `deliver

able: false`) — this covers both a
